title: RAG Concepts and Benefits
description: Understand retrieval-augmented generation, how it differs from fine-tuning, and why it is the dominant pattern for private-data AI in .NET backends.

blocks.text: Retrieval-augmented generation fetches relevant information from a trusted knowledge source and injects it into the LLM prompt at runtime. The model then generates an answer grounded in that context instead of relying on its training data alone.

blocks.title: When to use RAG versus fine-tuning

cards.title: RAG
cards.description: Retrieve external context at query time and inject it into the prompt.

cards.title: Fine-tuning
cards.description: Train the model on domain-specific examples before serving it.
cons: Hard to keep up with changing data

blocks.title: Simple RAG query flow in C#
blocks.content: A minimal RAG pipeline using Microsoft.Extensions.AI abstractions.

blocks.title: Rule of thumb
blocks.text: If your knowledge changes weekly, monthly, or per customer, prefer RAG. If you need the model to adopt a very specific style or domain reasoning pattern that is stable for months, fine-tuning may complement RAG.

blocks.title: Why RAG fits .NET backends well
items: **Private data stays private** — documents live in your database, not in model training data.
**Source attribution** — you can return citations with every answer.
**Control** — filter documents by tenant, user role, or document status before retrieval.
**Cost control** — reuse one model across many topics by changing the retrieved context.

blocks.title: Map Your Data to RAG
blocks.description: Identify a dataset in your work or studies that could benefit from question answering.
steps: Pick a document collection: API docs, support articles, or internal runbooks.
List the user questions that currently require human support.
Sketch how those documents would be chunked, embedded, and retrieved.
blocks.expectedOutcome: You should have a rough RAG design for a real dataset, including candidate chunk size and where metadata filters would help.
